answer: I built GHZ states of 2, 3, 4 and 5 qubits. A GHZ state is one where every qubit is entangled with all the others. A perfect machine would only ever give all 0s or all 1s, so every bit would agree. I ran all 4 circuits as one job of 100 shots each. I tested the job on the free sirius:mock first (job 01a1604d-d336-7535-a80b-907e5f93f2ec). It ran fine, but the mock only returns all-zero counts, so it checks the plumbing and not the physics. Then I ran one real job on sirius (job 01a1604d-f668-74b0-a334-7094fa539d9f). The API reports 1.0 billed second, which is about 0.3 credits. The fraction of shots where all bits agree was 0.96 for 2 qubits, 0.90 for 3, 0.83 for 4 and 0.77 for 5. A perfect machine would give 1.0 each time. The trend is that agreement drops as the state grows. Each extra qubit needs another entangling gate, and every gate and every readout has a small error rate. Those errors add up, so a bigger entangled state has more chances to get a bit flipped. The qubits also have more time to lose their quantum state as the circuit gets longer. The 5-qubit state still shows entanglement, since 77 of 100 shots were all 0s or all 1s. It is clearly worse than the 2-qubit state. Each size has only 100 shots, so each fraction carries a statistical error of roughly plus or minus 3 to 4 points, but the downward trend is steady. This is why noise limits how large an entangled state today's machines can make.
